1 The views expressed herein are a compilation of the views gathered from our member constituents and reflect the directional 
feedback of the majority of its collective members. CE has synthesized member feedback and the views, opinions, and positions 
should not be attributed to any single member and an individual member could disagree with all or certain views, opinions, and 
positions expressed by CE. 
 
 
June 15, 2026 
 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services, Attention: CMS-0062-P 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244-1850 
 
Submitted electronically at www.regulations.gov 
 
The Cooperative Exchange, the National Clearinghouse Association (CE), composed of 20 member 
organizations1, representing over 90% of the clearinghouse industry that supports over 1 million provider 
organizations, through more than 7,000 payor connections and 1,000 Health Information Technology (HIT) 
Vendors, and processes over 6 billion healthcare transactions annually; represents the U.S. healthcare 
electronic data interstate highway system enabling connectivity across all lines of healthcare eCommerce 
in the United States. We are pleased to comment on behalf of the Cooperative Exchange members on the 
proposed rule CMS-62-P, Medicare and Medicaid Programs: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, 
Medicaid Managed Care Plans, etc. 
Our members have significant experience in the exchange of health care transactions between and among 
providers and plans.  We are providing these comments based on our experience and knowledge of health 
care data exchange and our ability to facilitate that exchange.  Clearinghouses have and will continue to 
play an important role in the exchange of both administrative and clinical data.    
 
Comments on specific sections: 
Clearinghouse Role in Prior Authorization 
Section II.h.9 
There is a statement in the proposed rule (Section II.h.9) suggesting that clearinghouses do not play a role 
in prior authorization (PA) transactions.  However, clearinghouses currently process PA transactions today 
for providers and plans. In fact, the CE has recently launched a pilot program in cooperation with the DaVinci 
Trebuchet process to determine what changes in the PA implementation guides may be necessary to 
accommodate clearinghouse to clearinghouse exchange. The expected outcome of this collaboration with 
CE is to provide recommended updates to the Da Vinci implementation guides, which are critical to the 
success of the transactions our customers rely upon for processing, editing, and routing. We are happy to 
 
 
provide CMS with the results of our pilot test once available.  As such, we request that CMS note the current 
and active role of clearinghouses in PA transactions. 
 
Use of CRD for Eligibility Transaction Instead of 270/271 
Section II.h.6 
This inclusion of a prior authorization query as part of the eligibility transaction is unclear. It appears to 
adopt a second standard based on the "intent" of the query rather than the specific transaction itself.  
Specifically, traditional eligibility is triggered when an appointment is scheduled. CRD can also be triggered 
when an appointment is scheduled, and it is unclear from the proposal how a provider or their EHR/RCM 
system would know whether the intent is general benefit information or an inquiry on whether a prior 
authorization is required.  This could lead to unintentional violation of the HIPAA simplification rules which 
carry penalties for violators.  We suggest that CMS define a new transaction - a request from a provider to 
a health plan regarding the need for prior authorization for a specific service - and then adopt the CRD as 
the standard for that transaction.  This would clearly define the business process.  For clarity, we also 
suggest that CMS provide a specific example for this transaction.    
 
Use of FHIR for Referral Transactions Replacing 278 
Section II.h.2 
CMS proposed that the FHIR PAS specification be required for authorization referrals. Clearinghouses 
currently process millions of 278 referral transactions successfully, and few issues have been reported.    
Additionally, the FHIR transactions have not been pilot tested for referral, only for prior authorization, and 
CMS’ rules generally require that a standard at least be pilot tested before it is mandated in the HIPAA 
transaction set.  We do not believe that there is a need to replace the X12N TR3 278 for referrals and 
recommend only adopting the FHIR transactions for prior authorization.   
 
Eliminating the Direct Data Exception 
Section II.h.11 
We strongly recommend that CMS keep the direct data exception in place as an option for providers.  We 
have found that it serves a critical redundancy option for providers to use as they enroll in new plans and 
helps avoid disruptions when regular EDI channels have an issue. It is often preferred to make corrections 
to claims and to see results of payments before the remittance advice is received.  Providers using it today 
should continue to have the option, especially if they feel comfortable with it.  Health plans can choose to 
eliminate it if they wish but should not be required to. 
 
Endpoint Directory Reporting 
Section II.E 
We have concerns about whether the endpoint directory can be maintained with sufficient timeliness and 
accuracy to support its intended use. Clearinghouses can often identify broken or missing links due to the 
 
 
volume of transactions handled and our many connections to payers. Individual entities may not know 
issues as quickly.  We recommend that CMS provide a process for reporting issues with endpoints. 
While we are generally supportive of CMS maintaining a directory service, we believe the usefulness of 
such a directory is likely overestimated.  Any directory would need to be hierarchical and enable a single 
payer entity to have multiple endpoints for the same functionality, broken up by plan. Payers do not have a 
Unique Identifier, meaning that this type of structure will be very difficult to create and maintain.  
For prior authorization, payers are likely to have multiple endpoints for each plan for each of the different 
systems processing prior authorizations. Many payers outsource prior authorizations for specific service 
types to external partners while keeping some internally.  This could lead to a single plan under a 
payer having 3 or 4 different endpoints for prior authorizations. This is compounded by each plan having 
its own endpoints versus a single endpoint for the entire payer book of business. CMS can collect 
this information, but it will not solve the scale issues that point-to-point connections naturally have. 
 
Section III.B.2 
How do the enrollment and implementation processes for health care clearinghouses affect the 
health care industry’s ability to remain resilient? How could this be improved? 
The largest enrollment issues are with state Medicaid agencies and CMS Medicare/HETS. Clearinghouses 
have worked closely with commercial payers, Medicare Advantage plans, and Managed Care 
Organizations to streamline provider enrollment, but issues with the state and federal run gateways 
continue to persist. Within state Medicaid agencies, the biggest hurdle is the state gateway not allowing the 
transfer of provider enrollments from one TPID to another, even when owned by the same organization 
without the provider having to completely re-attest.  This makes it difficult to move providers between 
clearinghouses, or even between different platforms within the same clearinghouse organization, creating 
significant work for providers.  Additionally, CMS recently removed trading partner access to the 
HETS validation, preventing clearinghouses without a direct connection from validating through our 
intermediary if an NPI is correctly associated with our ID.  This change requires providers to go into the 
HETS tool and validate information, and make their own updates, significantly increasing provider 
burden.  Since this change, we have had multiple provider organizations unable to submit claims because 
they are unclear on what the new processes are and why their clearinghouse cannot provide 
the previous level of support.  Addressing both of these issues would significantly improve enrollment 
processes in the event a provider needs to quickly switch between clearinghouses or a clearinghouse 
needs to move a provider to a different internal platform. 
 
What are the potential benefits and challenges of a health care system with more point-to-point 
connections? 
While point-to-point connections work within a limited scope for very specific purposes, they simply are not 
capable of scaling nationwide to enable all providers easy exchange with payers.  The many-to-
many problem (thousands of providers and thousands of plans) in healthcare does not change simply 
because we now have FHIR APIs. Networks and clearinghouses address a specific set of 
challenges that block scaling of point-to-point transactions:  1) not all providers can natively generate 
compliant transactions (this is true even with FHIR), 2) not all payers accept transactions identically (payers 
have latitude to create companion guides requiring variations in the standards, including the new FHIR 
standards), 3) translation, validation, and routing remain necessary even with standards.  The FHIR 
 
 
standards are no more standardized than X12 or C-CDA, allowing for variation within each organization’s 
APIs. Additionally, payers do not have a single endpoint, but instead maintain endpoints setup at the plan 
level and, for prior authorization, may also rely on multiple partners to process authorization requests; as a 
result, this further compounds the many-to-many issue. Even in single payer health systems outside of the 
US, FHIR is being adopted in a network capacity because point-to-point cannot scale.        
 
What role do health care clearinghouses play in supporting point-to-point connections, and what 
role do they play in supporting the exchange of health care data? 
Clearinghouses support a contractual structure that is point-to-point (i.e. bilateral agreements between a 
provider and a payer) while supporting a technical structure that is networked. This provides the best of 
both worlds. Payers and providers do not squabble over data use rights because they are narrowly 
constrained in the bilateral agreements, and at the same time they have a single point of connection to 
reach all of the providers or payers they need to connect to, without having to modify their transaction 
formats to meet each connection’s requirements. This significantly reduces cost and speeds up 
implementation timelines for the industry.   Clearinghouses recognize the value of real-time transactions, 
with many clearinghouses already offering JSON APIs for eligibility and claim status, and most 
clearinghouses are embracing FHIR for prior authorization transactions.  To ensure clearinghouses can 
continue to transact with each other in a FHIR world, the Cooperative Exchange recently launched the 
Trebuchet Pilot Cohort for clearinghouse-to-clearinghouse prior authorization transactions.  
 
What options are available or recommended for streamlining transition processes, including 
moving from one health care clearinghouse to another, when one is impacted by a cyber attack? 
One of the primary challenges associated with transitioning between clearinghouses is the presence of 
exclusivity provisions and contractual lock-in terms. While some organizations have moved away from 
including these restrictions in their agreements, the practice is not yet universal across the industry. 
Should providers or payers need to transition clearinghouses unexpectedly or within a compressed 
timeframe, such provisions could create significant operational challenges. We recommend that 
clearinghouses avoid the use of exclusivity clauses in order to support greater flexibility, interoperability, 
and business continuity for providers and payers. 
 
Section III.C.2 
What aspects of API implementation pose the most significant implementation difficulties, and 
where do commenters perceive the potential for lack of conformance with the API technical 
requirements? 
Multiple versions of the FHIR implementation guides have been challenging as not all are backwards 
compatible. Coalescing to a single version and giving the industry time to adopt it would be helpful 
in addressing this challenge. The FHIR standards are advancing at a pace the industry is not prepared for, 
and a small slow down would enable broader adoption which would lead to better feedback and improved 
future versions.  Additionally, regardless of the work put in by the industry on the implementation guides, 
like all standards in the healthcare space there is significant variation allowed, and every implementer 
makes use of that allowance. APIs are not plug and play. On top of which the security standards wrapped 
around the FHIR APIs are solid but require significant work to enable point-to-point.   
 
 
 
What value would the certification of payer API technology provide to payers, providers, and 
patients? What would be the benefits and burdens of requiring certification of payer API technology 
for payers, providers, and patients?  
As has been demonstrated with the current certification program for APIs for provider systems, certification 
does not mean real-world performance.  Despite having certification criteria for FHIR APIs for 
years, anyone trying to connect to an EHR has to go through just as much work as they would without 
certification. It does not reduce implementation burden, and it increases cost for the entire industry. In 
contrast, CMS National Standards Group (NSG) performs real-world audits on HIPAA transactions to 
ensure compliance. The work effort for these on-the-spot audits is significantly lower, while also 
demonstrating that the standards are being followed in reality not just for a one-time certification.  We 
believe that this type of auditing would be more beneficial for providers, patients, and payers than a 
certification program. 
 
If ONC were to establish criteria for payer API technology, should CMS require certification to meet 
payer API requirements, or should such certification be made available solely on a voluntary basis? 
Would payers or developers of API technology providing solutions to payers be likely to obtain 
certification on a voluntary basis? 
We do not believe mandatory certification is valuable to the industry.  The ONC certification program, while 
well intentioned, has not ensured that APIs function in the real world versus in a testing environment. The 
program adds significant cost to building and maintaining products, unfairly advantaging large, long-
standing vendors, while disadvantaging new entrants, i.e. the certification program further entrenches the 
big players and stifles innovation.  Particularly with APIs that are not just query and retrieve but include 
multiple different workflows, it is unclear how the ONC certification program could even certify they function 
correctly.  
We 
believe 
that 
auditing, similar 
to what 
CMS 
NSG 
already 
performs 
for 
HIPAA transactions would be a better path forward for ensuring performance. 
 
 
General Concerns 
Regarding timing and reporting requirements for prior authorization, there is a need for accurate and 
consistent timestamping of transactions. We recommend that Implementation Guides and instructions 
assure that all transactions have timestamping requirements. 
Regarding enforcement, we request clarification on how compliance would be assessed when both a health 
plan and a clearinghouse are involved in delivering a prior authorization result that is untimely. Specifically, 
would CMS consider the health plan out of compliance if it transmits the result too late for the clearinghouse 
to meet the applicable timing requirements? We would appreciate additional guidance on how responsibility 
would be assigned in this scenario. 
 
We request that CMS publish information and tools for testing and conformance of these new FHIR 
requirements and future publications. 
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule.  If you have any questions, please have 
reach out to us at lisa@cooperativeexchange.org or phone at (205) 585-4000.
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** The Cooperative Exchange, the National Clearinghouse Association (CE).
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor / Clearinghouse industry association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents 20 member organizations, over 90% of the clearinghouse industry, more than 1 million provider organizations, more than 7,000 payer connections, 1,000 HIT vendors, and over 6 billion health care transactions annually.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The Cooperative Exchange supports the goal of electronic prior authorization but urges CMS to recognize clearinghouses as central infrastructure for scalable exchange. CE raises concerns about replacing or redefining existing HIPAA transactions without clear business process boundaries, warns that point-to-point API connections do not scale, recommends preserving the direct data exception, seeks a realistic endpoint directory process, opposes mandatory payer API certification in favor of real-world auditing, and asks for clearer timestamping, conformance tools, and responsibility rules when clearinghouses are involved.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS indirectly through timing/reporting; GENERAL/RFI — health care resiliency and payer API implementation; EXISTING-WORKFLOWS concerns.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Proposed rule sections II.h.9, II.h.6, II.h.2, II.h.11, II.E, III.B.2, III.C.2.
- **Standards referenced:** Da Vinci implementation guides, Da Vinci Trebuchet process, CRD, FHIR PAS, X12N TR3 278, X12 270/271 eligibility transaction, HIPAA administrative simplification standards, JSON APIs, FHIR, C-CDA, HETS, CMS National Standards Group audits.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Clearinghouse role in prior authorization**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** CE says clearinghouses already process PA transactions and are actively working with the Da Vinci Trebuchet process on clearinghouse-to-clearinghouse exchange.
- **Specific request:** CMS should recognize the current and active role of clearinghouses in PA transactions and consider CE pilot results.

**Topic 2: CRD and eligibility transaction ambiguity**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** CE argues that using CRD within or instead of an eligibility transaction based on query intent creates ambiguity and potential HIPAA administrative simplification violations.
- **Specific request:** CMS should define a new transaction for provider requests to health plans asking whether PA is required for a specific service, adopt CRD for that transaction, and provide a specific example.

**Topic 3: FHIR PAS for referrals and X12 278 replacement**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Oppose in part / Modify
- **Rationale:** Clearinghouses process millions of 278 referral transactions successfully, and CE says FHIR transactions have been pilot-tested for prior authorization but not referrals.
- **Specific request:** Do not replace X12N TR3 278 for referrals; adopt FHIR transactions only for prior authorization.

**Topic 4: Direct data exception**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Oppose elimination
- **Rationale:** Direct data entry provides redundancy during enrollment, EDI disruption, claim correction, and payment review workflows.
- **Specific request:** Keep the direct data exception available as an option for providers; permit plans to eliminate it voluntarily but do not require elimination.

**Topic 5: Endpoint directory reporting and scalability**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support with concerns / Modify
- **Rationale:** CE supports a directory in principle but warns that endpoint data may be hard to maintain accurately because payers often have multiple plan-level and service-specific endpoints and lack a unique payer identifier.
- **Specific request:** CMS should provide a process for reporting broken or missing endpoints and design any directory hierarchically to accommodate multiple endpoints per payer/plan/function.

**Topic 6: Clearinghouse resiliency and enrollment transitions**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** State Medicaid and CMS Medicare/HETS enrollment processes can impede continuity, and exclusivity/lock-in provisions can hinder rapid clearinghouse transitions during cyber events.
- **Specific request:** Improve transfer of provider enrollments between TPIDs, restore or address HETS validation support issues, and encourage clearinghouses to avoid exclusivity clauses.

**Topic 7: Point-to-point connection limitations**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** CE argues thousands of providers and plans create a many-to-many scaling problem that FHIR alone does not solve; validation, translation, routing, and network services remain necessary.
- **Specific request:** CMS should recognize the continued need for clearinghouse/network infrastructure rather than assuming point-to-point APIs can scale nationwide.

**Topic 8: FHIR implementation guide versioning and API conformance**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Multiple FHIR IG versions are challenging, not always backward compatible, and advancing faster than the industry can absorb; APIs are not plug and play.
- **Specific request:** Coalesce around a single version, give the industry time to adopt, slow the pace of standard changes, and publish testing/conformance information and tools.

**Topic 9: Payer API certification vs auditing**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Oppose mandatory certification
- **Rationale:** CE says certification does not ensure real-world performance, adds costs, advantages large incumbents, and may not work well for complex workflow APIs.
- **Specific request:** Use real-world auditing similar to CMS NSG HIPAA transaction audits instead of mandatory ONC payer API certification.

**Topic 10: Timestamping and enforcement responsibility**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Timing and reporting depend on accurate transaction timestamps and clear allocation of responsibility when both a plan and clearinghouse handle the PA result.
- **Specific request:** Require timestamping in implementation guides/instructions and clarify compliance responsibility when a health plan transmits a result too late for a clearinghouse to meet timing requirements.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** CE supports required standards only with clear business process boundaries, workable implementation guidance, and recognition of clearinghouse workflows.
- **S2:** CE says multiple FHIR IG versions are challenging and recommends coalescing around a single version.
- **S3:** CE asks CMS to give the industry enough time for adoption and avoid rapid, incompatible version transitions.
- **S23:** CE raises endpoint directory security/operational concerns indirectly by stressing accuracy, timeliness, and broken-link reporting.
- **S24:** CE recommends endpoint reporting accommodate multiple endpoints per payer, plan, function, and delegated PA partner.
- **S26:** CE implies endpoint information must be structured hierarchically to be useful.
- **S27:** CE stresses timeliness and a process for reporting endpoint issues.
- **S32:** CE discusses CRD ambiguity and recommends defining a distinct PA-required inquiry transaction.
- **S44:** CE supports FHIR for PA but not as a broad replacement for all adjacent transactions without testing and clarity.
- **S45:** CE recommends limiting FHIR adoption to prior authorization, not referrals.
- **S46:** CE asks CMS to preserve existing X12 278 referral workflows and direct data entry options where they work.
- **S47:** CE recommends more implementation time and slower standards advancement.
- **S50:** CE warns FHIR IGs and APIs are not plug-and-play and need conformance tools.
- **S54:** CE opposes mandatory certification and favors real-world auditing and conformance testing tools.
- **S55:** CE requests enforcement clarification where plans and clearinghouses share PA processing responsibilities.
- **S66-S82 / Resiliency and payer API RFIs:** CE describes clearinghouse enrollment barriers, point-to-point scaling limits, transition challenges during cyber events, API implementation difficulties, and the relative value of audits over certification.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Recognize clearinghouses' current and active role in PA transactions.
2. Use CE/Da Vinci Trebuchet pilot results to inform IG updates for clearinghouse-to-clearinghouse exchange.
3. Define a new transaction for determining whether prior authorization is required for a specific service and adopt CRD for that transaction.
4. Provide a concrete example of the CRD-based PA-required inquiry transaction.
5. Do not replace X12N TR3 278 for referrals; limit FHIR adoption to prior authorization where tested.
6. Preserve the direct data exception as a provider option.
7. Create a process for reporting broken or missing API endpoints.
8. Design endpoint reporting to handle multiple endpoints by payer, plan, function, and outsourced service partner.
9. Address Medicaid and HETS enrollment/validation barriers that limit clearinghouse resiliency.
10. Encourage clearinghouses to avoid exclusivity clauses and contractual lock-in provisions.
11. Recognize that clearinghouses/networks are needed for scalable many-to-many exchange even in a FHIR environment.
12. Coalesce around a single FHIR IG version and allow sufficient adoption time.
13. Prefer real-world audits over mandatory payer API certification.
14. Require accurate and consistent transaction timestamping.
15. Clarify plan vs clearinghouse responsibility for untimely PA results.
16. Publish information and tools for FHIR testing and conformance.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** CMS under-recognition of clearinghouses; ambiguity between eligibility and PA queries; untested FHIR referral replacement; endpoint directory accuracy; point-to-point scalability; incompatible IG versions; mandatory certification costs; unclear enforcement responsibility.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** HIPAA administrative simplification violations, disruption of working referral workflows, provider burden, claims submission failures, higher implementation costs, slower implementation, and reduced business continuity during cyber events.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Multiple payer endpoints, no unique payer identifier, plan-level and delegated PA processing, state Medicaid and HETS enrollment limitations, companion guide variation, non-backward-compatible IG versions, security implementation burden, exclusivity clauses, and variable API behavior.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** CE represents over 90% of the clearinghouse industry, supports over 1 million provider organizations, has more than 7,000 payer connections and 1,000 HIT vendor connections, and processes over 6 billion transactions annually.
- **Studies or research referenced:** CE references its Da Vinci Trebuchet pilot cohort but does not cite published studies.
- **Examples provided:** Provider enrollment transfer problems between TPIDs in state Medicaid gateways; HETS validation changes leading providers to be unable to submit claims; payers with multiple plan-level and service-specific PA endpoints; clearinghouses already offering JSON APIs for eligibility and claim status.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Clearinghouses, providers, payers, HIT vendors, state Medicaid agencies, CMS Medicare/HETS, patients indirectly, and API technology developers.
- **Economic implications:** Networked clearinghouse exchange reduces cost and implementation timelines; mandatory certification may increase costs and disadvantage new entrants; point-to-point infrastructure may impose unnecessary scale costs.
- **Technical feasibility:** CE sees FHIR PA adoption as feasible with clearinghouse participation, pilot testing, version stability, conformance tools, timestamping, and real-world auditing; it views point-to-point-only exchange as technically insufficient at national scale.
- **Patient care impact:** Indirect but meaningful: failed transactions, enrollment disruptions, or non-scalable APIs can delay administrative processing needed for care and coverage.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed / Concerned
- **Tone:** Technical, pragmatic, critical of specific proposals
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Clearinghouses currently process PA transactions today for providers and plans." - Context: CE rebuttal to any implication that clearinghouses do not play a PA role.
2. "We do not believe that there is a need to replace the X12N TR3 278 for referrals." - Context: Opposition to FHIR replacement for referral transactions.
3. "The many-to-many problem... does not change simply because we now have FHIR APIs." - Context: Argument that point-to-point APIs do not scale nationally.
4. "Certification does not mean real-world performance." - Context: Opposition to mandatory payer API certification.
5. "We recommend that Implementation Guides and instructions assure that all transactions have timestamping requirements." - Context: Timing and enforcement concern.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - CE asks CMS to slow FHIR version changes and give the industry time to adopt.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - CE warns certification and point-to-point implementation increase costs and burden.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Enrollment re-attestation, HETS validation changes, and loss of direct data options increase provider burden.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - CE discusses cyber-related clearinghouse transitions and API security implementation burdens.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The comment is heavily focused on FHIR, X12, endpoint, conformance, and scalability issues.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - CE says FHIR IGs have multiple incompatible versions and referrals have not been pilot-tested.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment emphasizes clearinghouse, payer, provider, vendor, CMS, and SDO coordination.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - CE recommends endpoint issue reporting, testing tools, and timestamping.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - CE seeks preservation of effective X12 278 referral and direct data workflows.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - The comment focuses on clearinghouses, HIT vendors, certification impacts, and market effects on new entrants.
